Hear, hear!
Fisheries Act

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING "CLOSE TIME", DEPOSITING OF WASTE, MARINE PLANTS, ETC.
speechtext:
He stated very definitely the opinion of the party he represents and exactly the views that I myself hold. It is interesting to examine this piece of legislation before us, Bill C-204. I believe we now have four ministers in the act; we have a front-line of four in the House. I have been trying to figure out how the other members of the cabinet could in some way or other find some constitutional excuse to become involved with legislation in the area of pollution. What will the Minister of Communications (Mr. Kier-ans) do to become involved in this field? What will the Solicitor General (Mr. Mcll-raith) and the Minister of Labour (Mr. Mack-asey) do? There must be some areas these ministers can move into with respect to pollution legislation. It seems it is the "in" thing now for ministers to bring in legislation in this particular area. It is as popular for ministers to move into this area as the yoyo was a few years ago.
I am not going to be critical of the bill; I think it is a good bill. It is a very simple piece of legislation; there is very little new in it. I guess the minister would be quick to point out, if I were to say there is nothing new in it, that it gives the minister a jump on the polluter in the sense that he can now demand that the potential polluter be forced to adopt certain procedures before causing pollution, whereas before this legislation existed-and we assume that it will obtain passage-a polluter could commit the act of pollution, after which he could be brought to task. The minister could point this out.
I have looked at the definitions in the bill and seen what is meant by pollution. I see, for example, that the previous legislation gave the minister authority to move in, prosecute and bring to task the people who were responsible for the tremendous amount of pollution which has taken place in almost every lake, stream and river in the Canadian nation up to the present time. Having looked at the bill, I am not overly impressed with the definition of intent. I will be much more impressed with the department's actions, based on the legislation. I suppose every Canadian over the years would have been more impressed if the government had taken more action to prosecute people who committed offences in this area.
I notice that the hon. member for South Shore this afternoon observed that the upper limit of the fine for anyone guilty of infringing the legislation is to be $5,000. I do not know why the minister built that limit into

April 20, 1970
Fisheries Act
the bill. Perhaps I am misinformed and not totally aware of all the intentions of the bill, but it seems to me that is a pretty small sum for a large company such as Erco of Canada, or any other large company which has been tried and found guilty of polluting, to pay. Even $5,000 per day is very little for them. On the other hand, it would be a pretty heavy fine for someone who is gutting codfish.
On looking at clause 6 of the bill I notice that there is reference to dragger operations off the Newfoundland coast. I do not think any member of the House will disagree with the need for that clause, because these drag-gers have been wreaking havoc in Newfoundland. Forcing them to stay outside the three-mile limit is a good thing, and I commend the minister for his thinking. This is in line with the commitment he made to the fishermen of Newfoundland and Atlantic Canada who have been plagued by these inshore dragging operations. I beg your pardon-I see the 12-mile limit is mentioned. This is commendable.
I was absolutely appalled at the statements made by the minister today and in his previous speeches about his department being in a position to police pollution. I believe that is the correct phrase and I believe I am quoting the minister correctly. He said the Department of Fisheries is now in a position to police pollution throughout the nation. If I were to say that this is unadulterated nonsense, I would not wish to be unnecessarily unkind to the Minister of Fisheries (Mr. Davis).
There are in Canada two major problems in this area. The first stems from the lack of intention on the part of the government to move decisively into this area. Pollution is becoming a real political issue and everybody, I think, wants to get into the act, including myself. A serious problem results from our not having the personnel who could police pollution.
The minister said this afternoon that there is in the Department of Fisheries an administrative arm that has the personnel and competent people to deal with pollution. He mentioned, I believe, river guardians and various officers who could move in as a team and deal with these problems.
No doubt he wants to leave the impression that we have an army of people ready to move in to catch offenders and bring the guilty to justice. Just to indicate the true state of affairs, may I say that last year there was a drastic reduction in the budget for river guardians and lake police, if you want

to call them that. I am referring to officers and guardians who are involved in apprehending offenders. We had a drastic reduction in the budget in this area. I cannot give the exact figures, although I have them in my office. I remember that there were reductions in some parts of Canada of almost 50 per cent in the number of guardians and people competent and capable of enforcing the law in this area.
May I talk about a river system I am familiar with? How would anyone like to see a beautiful river system such as the Gander River system, which includes a lake that is 25 miles long-and very beautiful it is-and a piece of very precious property belonging to the Canadian nation, inadequately policed? Several small rivers feed into that lake, and running out of that lake are 30 miles of beautiful river. This is one of the most prosperous pieces of salmon river, if I may say that, that we have.
Last year we had on occasions two guardians supposedly responsible for guarding the whole of the lake and river system. There ought to be many more than that responsible for this system. To bring this matter down to earth, may I say that I have fished on this river as a salmon fisherman since 1961 and never have I been asked to produce a licence, simply because nobody has been around to ask me to produce it.
Looking around now I see several hon. members in this House who have gone to my province and fished for salmon, and I hope many more will go back in future and fish on that beautiful river system. speechtext:
An hon. member shouted, "It's window-dressing". That could be the result of this piece of legislation. I challenge the minister on the matter of policing antipollution regulations. I challenge him to say in this House that there are sufficient personnel to enforce the regulations in this bill. Who is going to police the Canadian coasts? The minister is familiar with the west coast. There is the same situation on the east coast. There are tens of thousands of miles of coastline, bays and inlets where small pleasure craft can go on the west coast and where hardworking fishing craft can go on the east coast.
Who is going to board these craft and control their effluent? Who is going to watch what these craft dump into the sea? In one way this is reminiscent of legislation which says
Fisheries Act
you cannot replace a fuse in a fuse-box. Of course, nobody has fuse-boxes any longer. I ask the minister, who is going to enforce this law? The Canadian people are going to question the observations of the minister about his department's capability to police pollution. The minister should admit to the Canadian people that his department is not capable. More money, research and development is necessary to police pollution in Canada.
I rise to participate in this debate because of some unhappy experiences on the east coast with respect to recent pollution. I am sure all hon. members recall the Long Harbour situation where a whole bay was polluted and the livelihood of 400 fishermen was affected. These fishermen harvested good returns. People who had been making a decent living last year were faced with a whole bay of dead fish. The complete story was never told and I do not intend to exaggerate it because in many ways it is a dead issue.
Last year, when the Long Harbour situation was investigated, it was found to our dismay that the Department of Fisheries had acted in what I consider a totally irresponsible manner in permitting the particular plant to locate and pollute the whole environment without requiring any safeguards. I understand there was an exchange of letters and the company agreed that the effluent would be kept to a particular level of toxicity which would not be dangerous or hazardous to the fishlife. The government agreed to this. After the bay became polluted and the total fish population had been destroyed, this government department realized its mistake. There had been no built-in safeguards. The end result was that the company was forced to build centrifuges, settling-ponds and trailing-ponds to prevent pollution. The government should have assumed some financial responsibility initially and required that company to build in the necessary safeguards. In every location where that kind of industry developed, the results have been tragic so far as pollution of the environment is concerned. Thousands of Canadian citizens, not scientists or researchers, could have made that information available to the minister from experience which they gained not far from Ottawa.
There is also the Arrow incident, which has been the subject of many discussions in this House. A couple of days ago I noticed in the Globe and Mail a picture of the Minister of Transport (Mr. Jamieson) devouring nice, juicy lobster from that particular area. I

I have been in every Canadian province. In the last five or six years I have travelled extensively in Canada. I am not familiar with the environment in each province, but I do know that my native province of Newfoundland is one of the most pollution-free provinces in Canada. In order to attract tourists we brag about the fact that we are one of the few unmolested areas in Canada. Our province is one of the few virgin areas with beautiful lakes, rivers, streams and pounds. speechtext:
No, it was not out of season. I caught these 21 brook trout in about

an hour. If you become thirsty when fishing there, you can drink the beautiful clear waters. One does not appreciate this situation unless he leaves and then returns. I can appreciate it because I must drive past the Ottawa River every day. I do not envy anyone who has to do that. I appreciated returning to the east coast, standing by a beautiful little lake and catching 12 or 15 eastern lake trout or mud trout. This can be done in many thousands of areas in Newfoundland today. The situation is even better in Labrador. However, things are happening which are causing concern. I doubt if my children will be able to do the things I was able to do in my childhood.
e (9:20 p.m.)
The Exploit river system was one of the most productive salmon systems on the east coast of Canada but today, I understand, it is almost completely dead. As I say, it was a beautiful system but today it is just about dead. I asked the minister whether he will conduct an investigation of the Gander system. I have received correspondence from him, and he agreed with some of my conclusions. There is scarcely a pond, stream, bay or inlet in Canada right across the whole nation where pollution will not be found to exist. This is a major issue. I support this legislation, but the minister should be given the necessary funds and authority to do the job properly. If not, let him leave it until the necessary funds are available.
Another problem has been presented by the decision to set up a petrochemical complex in Come-by-Chance. This is the news of the year; it is to be a $130 million complex. To my knowledge, Mr. Speaker, not a single piece of research has been done by the Department of Fisheries on the effect on the environment of a project of this kind. I do not say we have no need for a petrochemical plant; God knows, we need such developments, even developments of a type one would not normally want in one's backyard. But the least the government could do would be to assure the Canadian nation that an

establishment of this kind will not destroy the surrounding environment. I ask the minister to assure us that his official will look into this aspect, and that all the necessary pollution control equipment is built into the operation immediately. In the time left to me I wish to comment on the speech made by my hon. friend from South Shore. Perhaps the main point he made concerned the question of responsibility. We have heard a good deal this year from the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources. I sometimes have the feeling that this minister is the big boss in the cabinet where pollution control is concerned. After all, he was a candidate for the leadership and I do not doubt there is an overflow effect. His campaign met with a good measure of success and he was likely one of the keys to the election of the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau). speechtext:
I am interested in supporting the minister. Mr. Speaker, the "phosphate kid," the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources, has been using the phosphate issue as the best political gambit I have seen since I entered politics. He has almost succeeded in convincing the Canadian nation that if we can prevent these phosphates entering our waters we shall have beaten pollution. This is a complete misrepresentation of the facts, but it is a beautiful job.
The hon. lady for Vancouver-Kingsway (Mrs. Maclnnis) almost finds herself supporting the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources in his present effort. Editorials all over the country are supporting the minister in his fight against phosphate pollution. But the fact of the matter is-and the Minister of Fisheries agrees with me-that phosphate pollution is not even a major problem; it is
Fisheries Act
relatively easy to control. Indeed, phosphates are a form of nutrient which might well benefit certain species of fish. The minister himself has acknowledged this.
Here we have a minister who is responsible for a water act which may never come into effect, and if it does, he may have no control over it. Five Canadian provinces have stated that they do not intend to play any role under the permissive legislation proposed by the "green" Minister of Energy. I understand Ontario is the latest province to indicate it wants no part of this bill; they have more effective control through their own commission than through the toothless, gormless legislation proposed by the Minister of Energy. They recognize there is no money. They recognize there is a lot of political hay being made, that it will not result in the setting up of one, universal, authoritative body; they recognize it will be so diluted as a result of the discretion permitted by the act as to be totally ineffective.
Now we find the Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. Chretien) concerned in this field. Can anyone imagine the Minister of Indian Affairs having legislative authority in regard to pollution? I have been reminded of something by my hon. friend from St. John's East who spoke at the United Nations last year and recommended that control of pollution should be one of the key projects of the United Nations, recognizing in advance the extent of the problem.
[DOT] (9:30 p.m.)
My hon. friend from St. John's East reminds me that last year at the International Conference at Brussels our representative was the Minister of Transport. He brought back a report which I have in my hand. It is the statement of the Minister of Transport to the Brussels Conference on Pollution of the Sea by Oil, and is dated November 10, 1969.
When the minister returned to the House, if I am not mistaken he was questioned by hon. members and agreed he was going to bring in some anti-pollution legislation. Indeed, he is already moving in this area in regard to the regulations in connection with the voyage of the Manhattan.
We therefore have involved in pollution control the Minister of Energy, the Minister of Indian Affairs and the Minister of Transport. This piece of legislation, Bill C-204, has been brought in under the name of the Minister of Fisheries. The hon. member for South Shore has reminded us today that we have a

April 20, 1970
Fisheries Act
problem-a ship called "Pollution" which is being manned by three captains. I disagree
with him. I contend the ship is being manned by four captains, with all kinds of other captains in the wings who will be coming forward as the years go by and the ship pulls further out to sea. One hon. member asked this afternoon in which direction the ship would be going, and somebody responded that it would be going down. I would agree with that observation.
I have read Bill C-204 and it has all the
ingredients for very good legislation. I do not think there is any major change being made. I firmly believe that the only major change is that it permits the minister to act in advance in order to head off pollution. I think I am right in saying that. The legislation permits the minister to sort of head off pollution; it prevents pollution taking place rather than punishes after the event. The legislation is more preventive than punitive, if I may summarize it in that way.
Other than redefining waste and disposal of waste, I see nothing new in this legislation. In addition, I agree with the intent of the legislation. But I disagree that we are able to police pollution. Neither do I see why we must have three other ministers dragged into the fight against pollution. I have confidence in this minister; I think he is capable.

speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: AMENDMENTS RESPECTING "CLOSE TIME", DEPOSITING OF WASTE, MARINE PLANTS, ETC.
speechtext:
The government has the constitutional authority to make the minister in charge of the Department of Fisheries responsible for pollution control. In that regard I am quoting the minister, and I am fully aware of his position. I am also aware of his interest. He is an expert in his own field. Anybody who knows the Minister of Fisheries knows that. However, I do not want to praise him too much because he is also a very modest man.
The act is a simple one. The question here is one of defining what is going to be done. It is a question of allocating resources so we can do the necessary policing, of getting the personnel to enforce this particular piece of legislation. Again I ask why we need to drag into this field the Minister of Energy, Mines and Resources, who as far as I am concerned has very little knowledge of pollution control outside of the fact that he talks a lot about the Great Lakes. Of course the Great Lakes are polluted; they have been for generations.

Pollution has much broader aspects than that. I am concerned about pollution of salt water, the Pacific Ocean and the Atlantic Ocean. The Minister of Fisheries' department is geared to this kind of pollution control. The department has the necessary professional staff and the departmental structure to fight pollution in the broad sense. It is also geared to fighting pollution in the specific sense in which control is now delegated to the Minister of Energy.
I also suggest the Minister of Indian Affairs has no business to poke his nose into this affair, and the Minister of Transport has enough problems of his own. It is against all sound managerial concepts and sound principles of control and authority in the field of business management, in industry-you name it-to make four or five people responsible for tackling a particular problem, one which is relatively simple to define though somewhat more difficult to police, and much more difficult to allocate resources to meet.
I suggest we do not need the Canada Water Act. The act is a nebulous document, one which is totally ineffective. The provinces do not want it and the minister cannot enforce it. The legislation has no teeth. We want pollution control placed where it belongs, under the Department of Fisheries. We want the responsibility for fighting pollution to lie with the Minister of Fisheries. I do not envy him this role because it would be a major one. I think the Fisheries Act can provide the policing, the personnel and the resources effectively to take action against one of the major enemies of modern society in this twentieth century.
I cannot close on a stronger note than to support 100 per cent the observations made by the hon. members for South Shore, St John's East and South Western Nova in regard to some kind of single authority being vested in one minister, instead of fragmenting and dividing authority to the point where the whole government is made responsible for pollution control. We tried to get away from this sort of thing in the area of regional economic expansion and have been fairly successful. But we are now moving back to it again in the area of pollution control.

Mr. Speaker, when I heard the hon. member for Gander-Twillingate (Mr. Lundrigan) saying all those nice things about the Minister of Fisheries and Forestry (Mr. Davis) I began to wonder whether he was a Liberal backbencher.
April 20, 1970

The Minister of Fisheries made a number of statements this winter in regard to the fisheries. I noticed that they were very similar in content to one he made today and which appears in a press release. He said that healthy fish mean a healthy environment, and a healthy fishery is undoubtedly the best insurance policy we can buy in our battle against pollution in water.
I can understand why the minister makes statements of a similar nature because we have had a number of bills this session that are somewhat similar in nature. When I hear the minister speaking about fish, and so on, I cannot help thinking he had wished that Merlin the magician had touched them with his magic wand so that he really understood how the fish themselves felt and thought. From what he says, one would think he had a fair understanding of fish. I think it is reasonable to equate healthy fish with a healthy environment, and the same could be said of other statements made by the minister.
In view of the great variety of legislation dealing with pollution control that the House is dealing with at the moment, I think if I were a fish I would not be sure just which bill presently before the House was polluting me or was not polluting me. Even as a Member of Parliament I am a little confused as to which bill will deal with which part of Canada.

speechtext:
Yes. While we are all in favour of anti-pollution measures, I feel that some of these questions may work themselves out in time. At the moment it seems there is some confusion, particularly over the question of authority, as to how these particular bills are going to operate. For example, the minister suggested that the present bill would be dovetailed into the Canada Water Act. If I were a fish, I would say to him that he would probably water it down. It seems to me that some aspects of pollution control, at least, will not be as effective as would be the case if control was kept within the fisheries legislation we are now discussing. I feel that since the Canada Water Act requires the co-operation of the provinces and regional authorities, pollution control would not be nearly as effective as it would be under one authority.
[DOT] (9:40 p.m.)
I should like to mention one thing in respect of section 33A in which it is stated that the Minister of Fisheries and Forestry
Fisheries Act
will have control in respect of plants in certain areas. A plant, for example, situated on the Fraser River, presumably under the authority of the Canada Water Act, could pass its effluent into the river. The effluent would then pass down into the Pacific Ocean, where it would come under the authority of the Minister of Fisheries and Forestry. It seems to me there is a conflict here. This water would come under the control of the minister after something has happened to it, and it would be his job to clean it up.
I suggest this is a backward move. I believe the reverse should be the situation and that the minister should have authority over the whole region. It would seem that the regional authority would lack the co-operation of many individuals and that the Minister of Fisheries and Forestry would have to clean up the water when it reached Vancouver Harbour or the mouth of the Fraser River. I think there might well be some conflict here. I suggest that the minister look into this particular situation to see whether or not further amendments are called for.
For a moment I should like to speak about drilling for oil off the shores of Canada because I understand this matter will be covered by some portion of this bill. I do not quite go along with members representing the Atlantic coast who say there should be no drilling at all for oil. I think his might be desirable in areas where there is a fault such as was the case in respect of Santa Barbara. I suggest that if sufficient precautions were exercised, such as adequate wellhead procedures and control measures, we could continue to drill for oil. I think that if proper procedures were followed we could drill for oil and look after our pollution problem at the same time. I believe that with the high living in society there will be some pollution risk. I am against pollution as much as anyone, but I believe we should be realistic and realize that oil will continue to be used in buses, aeroplanes and motor cars.
It has been suggested by other speakers that there should be more research in various areas concerning pollution control. It seems to me there may be some conflict in respect of our various pollution control measures. It would seem to me also that a need for arbitration in this regard might arise some time in the future unless something is done about this problem. Just the other day I noticed snow and salt on the ice of a river. Presumably this will go into the water and pollute it. Perhaps it is a little thing, but in any event it is part of the problem.

April 20, 1970
Fisheries Act
I should like to compliment the minister on the bill. I believe other people today have pointed out some of the problems in relation to it. We hope the minister will consider these suggestions and come up with amendments, not necessarily at this session-although it might be that some changes are necessary now-but perhaps next year if it should be found that changes are necessary.
There is one good thing about this bill which I should like to mention. As I read it, the control in respect of pollution will remain in the hands of the Minister of Fisheries and Forestry until such time as the regional authority comes into effect. I believe this is a very good provision. We do not know how long it will be before these various water management agencies come into effect. speechtext:
Thank you, Mr. Speaker. I am somewhat overwhelmed by some of the kind remarks expressed today about the Fisheries Department and the effective way in which it has been carrying out its duties. I hope we can have the support of all parties in the House in getting this legislation through quickly, but in saying that I do not mean that we should put it through precisely in the form in which it has been introduced. I hope we can improve on it in some way, although I am not certain how. But I am sure that some of the questioning in the committee will produce ideas whereby we can strengthen the bill still further.
I think that the Fisheries Act as amended will be a sharp instrument, a specific tool which we can use to deal with spot situations across the country. I also think it creates standards which are essentially nationwide and, as I said earlier, these will prevent the development of pollution havens which tend to exist in the economically weaker areas of the country.
The question was asked as to why the old sections of the Fisheries Act dealing with pollution had not been enforced more rigorously down through the years. The sections in question were all too embracing, all too comprehensive. For instance, anyone who threw sawdust, bark or lime into a stream could be prosecuted. As the years and decades went by and prosecutions were not laid, it became more and more difficult to enforce legislation of this kind. In other words, it withered away; it fell into disuse, and indeed we failed ourselves in not using it more effectively.
What we really need in legislation of this kind is not an absolute prohibition on everything thrown into our waters but more precise measurements of what can be thrown into water and still keep it clear, clean and useful to the fisheries, and being useful to the fisheries healthy for men and women as well. In other words, we need to know what con-22218-39
Fisheries Act
centrations of a whole range of materials are tolerable, and what concentrations of those materials are not tolerable.
By introducing the word "waste" into the legislation, and by defining in the regulations the concentrations of the various chemicals which can or cannot be tolerated in the fisheries waters of Canada, we will have a more precise and useful tool in legislation which can be enforced throughout the country equitably and effectively. There are various kinds of wastes, not all of which affect fish and not all of which kill fish. The Fisheries Act, as it has been administered, by and large required the evidence of fish that were killed or of fish that were seriously affected by pollutants. Not all chemicals affect fish. Phosphates in some concentrations encourage plant life in the water and may not be too detrimental to fish, but obviously they create unsightly ponds, and so on. Therefore, phosphates have to be dealt with under other legislation.
The Fisheries Act does not solve all the problems. It does not necessarily solve the problem of effluents from municipalities, but it certainly deals with most industrial pollutants. The pulp and paper industry, with some 180 mills across the country, puts the greatest single burden on Canada's rivers and streams. Perhaps 60 per cent of the burden of pollution from industry is placed on Canadian streams by the pulp and paper industry. In fact, a single mill can create as much burden on a river as a city the size of Ottawa does. We can deal in large measure with pollutants from pulp and paper mills through the Fisheries Act. We can deal with the greater part of industrial pollution from chemical plants, from most chemical processing industries, and from many mines. As I say, the Fisheries Act can be used in large measure to deal with pollutant problems which arise from industry but not necessarily from municipalities.
One hon. member mentioned a specific oil refinery to be built at Come-By-Chance in Newfoundland. We are already in touch with the people there, but I would suggest that with the amendments to the Fisheries Act we have the law behind us when we ask for information. If the plans which we discuss with that refinery, or with other refineries, do not meet the standards which our people believe are required to clean up the effluent, then with the agreement of the cabinet by Order in Council we can stop construction until the company in question agrees to

April 20, 1970
Fisheries Act
instal the type of equipment which has been proven effective elsewhere. This is the sort of thing which is contemplated in the bill.
An oil-drilling rig being set up in any of the fisheries waters of Canada would be like a new plant being built on a major salmon stream in another part of the country. We can similarly ask for their plans and their precautions, for information on the processes which they will follow in order to protect the living resources of the water. If the plans, the location and the over-all situation are such as to give the Department of Fisheries real concern, then possibly we can stop the drilling from going ahead.
Mention was made of water quality management areas. In a number of situations, particularly where there are a number and a variety of industries, where there are one or more municipalities, where there is a wide range of ac ivities and a multiplicity of effluents we need the powers not only of one department of the federal government, namely, the Department of Fisheries, but also the powers of the Canada Shipping Act, the powers under our national health legislation, the powers under all the provincial pieces of legisla ion and the powers of municipal bylaws. We need the full force of all the legislative powers and administrative abilities of all three levels of government in such situations, and this in good measure is where the Canada Water Act comes in.
Many hon. members have alluded to the possibility that we could in a sense be downgrading our fisheries powers through this bill, especially with reference to the Canada Water Act and its water control management areas and agencies, but certainly as long as I am Minister of Fisheries, and as long as many of the officers of the department hold their present positions I can say that we are not going to back up one single step when we insist on proper fisheries standards. We are going to make sure that the fisheries standards still ob'aining generally across the country, ob ain in those areas. Some other standards, not necessarily fisheries standards, will apply as well. I would suggest that we will have cleaner water and better conditions for fish in those situa'ions of joint enterprise, joint management and federal, provincial and municipal co-operation in the water quality management areas.
[DOT] (10:00 p.m.)
The Northern Inland Waters Act was mentioned. The powers which the Minister of

Indian Affairs and Northern Development (Mr. Chretien) is asking for under that legislation are similar to those enjoyed by a provincial government, for example, the water right powers. A province could authorize the development of a mine and thus inadvertently authorize something harmful to the local fishery. If a dispute occurs between the Department of Indian Affairs and Northern Development and the Department of Fisheries and Forestry, there is a clause in the Fisheries Act which allows it to be resolved around the cabinet table, and if this should occur I hope the Minister of Fisheries and Forestry would carry the day in the cabinet chamber.
Mention was made that a $5,000 fine was inadequate, for example in relation to the Electric Reduction Company in Newfoundland. We did not fine the Electric Reduction Company in order to make retribution for the so-called "red herring" incident in Newfoundland. We asked the company to clean up and it met all our standards. It also finally compensated the fishermen and we expect to recover all our loans. In all, I would say the company was out of pocket nearly $2 million. The company could have avoided this with good planning at the outset.
Before I conclude I shall answer the hon. member for Gander-Twillingate (Mr. Lundri-gan). With the present personnel of the Department of Fisheries and Forestry I do not believe we have enough people to police pollution across Canada. We expect to get help from other departments and municipalities but we need some more staff, particularly competent engineers with knowledge about the optimum design of treatment facilities. We also need more people on the mercury program and more of the machines developed in the last 12 to 18 months that enable us to find the parts per million of mercury in fish. Without that equipment we could never have discovered this problem.
In summary, Mr. Speaker, the Fisheries Act is a sharp federal tool and one which we can use effectively to deal with pollu ion problems, especially those arising in industry. We cannot solve all the problems, but we can co-operate with other departments of the government in tackling pollution on the broadest possible front. I welcome comments, criticisms and suggestions for improvement in the legislation when we meet in committee.

HOUSING-SUSPENSION OF CMHC LOANS IN LARGER CITIES
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, on March 13 I asked the Minister wi.hout Portfolio in charge of housing (Mr. Andras) if he could tell the House whether Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation has cut off housing loans in cities of over 10,000 population and, if so, why? I am sure the answer the Minister without Portfolio gave me at that time was, to his way of thinking, adequate to fit the needs at that particular time.
I am also certain the minister realizes that the people in the area I come from have run into a situation where there is no private money available. Contractors have made application to Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation for money and have been told there is no money under the regulation alluded to. There is no private money available for the type of condominium construction being talked about.
One of the main matters that all of us must be concerned about is that several departments of government, particularly the Department of Regional Economic Expansion, are attempting to look after various aspects concerning the whole country and trying to bring about development in some areas of Canada, whereas at the same time Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation is not permitting development in those areas which are under the jurisdiction of regional economic development programs.
I appreciate that the Minister without Portfolio in charge of housing has said to the mayor of Moose Jaw that the government is looking at this matter and will examine any proposals that proponents may wish at this time to bring forward. At the same time we realize that it is not good enough when only two areas in Saskatchewan are to be entitled to any consideration under this legislation.

This is really the reason behind my raising this question tonight. I say this because there is no way that some areas may obtain assistance from private lenders. It is common knowledge that Central Mortgage and Housing leads the way with lending. It appears that private lenders sort of bend their ear to learn what Central Mortgage and Housing Corporation is doing, and under those conditions private lenders will look at any enterprise or any type of construction only if it fits into plans concerned with regional economic development. I hope the Minister without Portfolio will give an assurance that he will look at this matter in a very serious manner and will say, in the short time he has available, whether the government will be looking at legislation which will assist communities across the nation in this regard.

speakeroldname: Hon. Robert K. Andras (Minister without Portfolio):

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I will do my best to respond to the hon. member. In the allocation
of the $854 million that I described on February 2, I believe, in this House I made the point that section 40 loans, which generally speaking are loans at market interest for individual people building or acquiring houses, had been reduced very considerably from previous years and stand this year at $110 million.
The purpose of this was to allocate much more money and give much greater emphasis to social housing programs such as public housing and section 35 and section 16 housing, those being so-called limited dividend, non-profit operations. We then put $570 million into those other programs, $265 million going into public housing, and this is in turn distributed to the various provinces. That, I think, includes an acceptably generous allocation to the province of Saskatchewan which certainly matches the request that the province had made. It, in turn, totally administers this money in terms of selecting priority of location and the submission of projects, and we do not turn them down except for obvious reasons involving concentration density, style, physical form and so on. But it is totally at the discretion of the provincial government to allocate that money to the various communities.

speakeroldname: Mr. E. F. Whelan (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Fisheries and Forestry):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Fisheries and Forestry
maintopic: HISTORIC SITES-ACQUISITION OF RESIDENCE OF SIR ROBERT BORDEN
speechtext:
I do
not intend to try to answer in the eloquent terms which the hon. member has used, Mr. Speaker. This house was designated by the minister as being of national historic significance upon recommendation of the Historic Sites and Monuments Board of Canada. The board recommended that every effort be made to preserve the building and that it be marked by a plaque. Having studied Sir Robert Borden's life a little, I think he might have been glad that the area where he lived should provide accommodation for so many people in need of homes.
DEBATES	6093
Proceedings on Adjournment Motion
It is my understanding that shortly after the designation of the house by the minister as being of national significance, it was sold by the previous owner, a foreign government, to a developer for use as the site of a high-rise apartment building. This developer has, I believe, now commenced demolition of the house and it is my understanding that the roof is already partially removed and the interior gutted. I am sorry to say, therefore, that it is in fact too late to preserve the house.
It should be mentioned that designation of a house by the minister as being of national significance does not imply any obligation on the part of the minister to ensure that such a building continues to be preserved, although it does imply an effort at preservation. A number of buildings of this kind have been thus designated by the minister in recent years and very often the act of designation has ensured the preservation of the house by local interests. In some instances co-operative agreements have been entered into with local groups whereby costs of preservation have been shared.
In this instance it is, unfortunately, too late to take any appropriate action. Even if action had been feasible it must be pointed out that it would have cost almost half a million dollars to acquire the house and ensure its preservation, and this sum would have been disproportionately high in relation to the total budget of the National Historic Sites Service. I would further mention that the Historic Sites and Monuments Board of Canada is well aware that the department operates on a very limited budget for historic preservation, especially at this time. The budget for contingencies is necessarily a very small one and there were no funds available at the time the emergency arose concerning the demolition of this house.
